Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A square matrix [MATH: A] is block diagonalizable if it is similar to a block diagonal matrix [MATH: B.] That is, there exists a block diagonal matrix [MATH: B] and an invertible matrix [MATH: P] such that

Content:
[MATH: A=PBP^{-1}.]

Content:
For example, the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [2|0|0; − 2|3|2; − 1|− 2|3]]

Content:
is block diagonalizable because it can be factored as follows:

Content:
[MATH: [2|0|0; − 2|3|2; − 1|− 2|3]]

Content:
Here, the matrix [MATH: A] has eigenvalues

Content:
[MATH: {\color{red}\lambda_1 = 2},\qquad
{\color{blue}\lambda_2=3-2\textrm i},\qquad
{\color{blue}\lambda_3=3+2\textrm i}.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: \lambda_2 = \overline{\lambda_3}.]
The eigenvectors of [MATH: {\color{red}\lambda_1}, {\color{blue}\lambda_2},] and [MATH: {\color{blue}\lambda_3},] respectively, are

Content:
[MATH: [1; 0; 1]]

Content:
Again, notice that [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2 = \overline{\mathbf{v}_3}.]
The first column of [MATH: P] corresponds to the eigenvector [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1},] and the second and third columns correspond to the real and the imaginary parts of [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Block Diagonalization Theorem for a 3x3 Matrix

Content:
We have the following theorem regarding the block diagonalization of a real [MATH: 3\!\times\! 3] matrix:

Content:
> If [MATH: A] is a real [MATH: 3\times 3] matrix with one real eigenvalue [MATH: {\color{red}\lambda_1}] with corresponding eigenvector [MATH: {\color{red}{\mathbf{v}_1}},] and two complex eigenvalues [MATH: {\color{blue}\lambda_2} = \overline{\color{blue}\lambda}_{\color{blue}3}] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} = \overline{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}_{\color{blue}3},] then
> [MATH: A=PBP^{-1},]
> where the matrices [MATH: B] and [MATH: P] are given by
> [MATH: λ_{1}|0|0; 0|Re(λ_{2})|Im(λ_{2}); 0|− Im(λ_{2})|Re(λ_{2})]

Content:
In other words, if [MATH: A] is a real [MATH: 3\!\times\! 3] matrix with one real eigenvalue and two complex eigenvalues, then [MATH: A] is block diagonalizable.

Content:
Note the following:

- The block of [MATH: B] constructed from the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: \color{blue}\lambda_2] is a rotation-scaling matrix.
- We can write the blocks of [MATH: B] in either order. However, the order of the columns of [MATH: P] must correspond to the order of the blocks.
